Typical presentation is subacute or gradual onset of pain in the scrotum; patients may have fever or urinary symptoms. C
Physical examination typically reveals localized epididymal tenderness, normally oriented testicle and presence of cremasteric reflex. C

Must evaluate for testicular torsion if pain is of acute onset or severe, the testicle is diffusely tender or horizontally oriented, there is an absent cremasteric reflex, or any other suspicion for torsion. C
Color duplex Doppler ultrasound can differentiate between testicular torsion and epididymitis, but referral to a urologist should not be delayed by imaging if torsion is suspected. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Acute, severe pain; high-riding transversely-oriented testicle; negative cremasteric reflex
Entire testicle swollen and painful; positive cremasteric reflex

list.listitem: Patients typically present with gradual onset of unilateral scrotal pain with radiation to the abdomen; fever (~75%) and urinary symptoms (~33%) may accompany (dysuria, frequency, hematuria). May rarely be bilateral. Coexisting orchitis is common, as is erythema of the scrotal skin.

Testicle is in normal position and cremasteric reflex is present in epididymitis. High-riding, transversely-oriented testicle (LR+ 46), absence of cremasteric reflex (LR+ 8.5), and presentation within 6 hours of onset suggests testicular torsion.
Presence of fever and/or urinary tract symptoms support the diagnosis of epididymitis. Relief of pain with elevation of the testicle (Prehn's sign) also supports a diagnosis of epididymitis.
In torsion, onset is usually more sudden and severe. Any patient with acute scrotal pain and possible torsion requires emergent referral to a urologist.

Test for gonorrhea and chlamydia in all males between the ages of 14 years and 35 years and if there is a new sexual partner at any age. Obtain a urine specimen for urinalysis and culture. Peripheral leukocytosis was seen in 64% in one series of 121 patients with acute epididymitis and supports the diagnosis.

Color duplex Doppler ultrasound is an accurate test for torsion and acute epididymitis but ordering imaging should not delay referral to a urologist for surgical exploration if torsion is suspected. Ultrasound is 93% sensitive and 92% specific for acute epididymitis; radionuclide imaging has similar accuracy.
In one small study, use of a hand-held Doppler showing absence of Doppler arterial signals predicted torsion.

In one series of 172 boys with acute scrotal pain (41 of whom had torsion), 3 findings predicted torsion: duration of pain less than 6 hours, absent or decreased cremasteric reflex, and diffuse testicular tenderness.
If all 3 were absent, no boys had torsion. If all 3 were present, 87% had torsion.
Between the ages of 14 years and 35 years, treat presumptively for gonorrhea and chlamydia with ceftriaxone 500 mg IM plus doxycycline 100 orally twice daily for 10 days. B

For patients younger than 14 years and older than 35 years, or with allergy to cephalosporins or tetracyclines, treatment with ofloxacin 300 mg orally twice daily or levofloxacin 500 mg orally once daily for 10 days is recommended. B
Supportive care with ice, scrotal elevation, analgesics and rest is probably beneficial. C

Between the ages of 14 years and 35 years (gonorrhea or chlamydia likely): CDC guidelines recommend ceftriaxone 500 mg IM once plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 10 days. Cefixime and azithromycin are no longer recommended due to increased gonorrheal resistance.

Age less than 14 or more than 35 years (enteric organisms likely) and those allergic to cephalosporins and/or tetracyclines: CDC guidelines recommend ofloxacin 300 mg orally twice daily for 10 days or levofloxacin 500 mg orally daily for 10 days.
A systematic review only found 1 RCT for the treatment of acute epididymitis, highlighting the importance of conducting more prospective trials comparing different treatment regimens.
Immunocompromised patients require no alteration in therapy.
Analgesics as needed.
Scrotal elevation, limitation of physical activity, and ice may be helpful but have not been studied in clinical trials.
Refer urgently for suspected testicular torsion.
Also consider referral for suspected abscess, chronic epididymitis, testicular mass, and any prepubescent males with anatomic abnormalities.
Most patients improve symptomatically within 1 to 3 days. Complication rate is unknown but likely very low. C
Reevaluate in 3 to 7 days to ensure resolution of pain/tenderness and to evaluate for testicular mass. C
Evaluate and treat sexual partner if gonorrhea or chlamydia are suspected or diagnosed. C
